extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; scholars of 18th-century journalism, drama, and humor; writers interested in comic writing and periodical essaycraft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and adapting comic drama and periodical humorous essays in the English (early-18th-century) tradition — covering tone, moral content, theatrical technique, and audience-sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse language and oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's comedies were 'wholly free from the garnish of oaths and unwholesome expletives which his contemporaries seemed to think essential to stage emphasis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that does not rely on profanity or coarse expletives for force; keep comic dialogue clean rather than using rough emphasis as a crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should be grounded in seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Each comedy of his was based on seriousness, as all sound English wit has been since there have been writers in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underneath gaiety and humour, maintain a substratum of earnest thought or moral seriousness to give the wit substance and social purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's 'Christian Hero' was felt to be 'too didactic' — an air of superiority, allowed to the professional man teaching rules of his own art, belongs to a too didactic manner and is repugnant to Steele's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let instruction or moralizing take the tone of sermonizing; prefer indirectly instructive or exemplifying approaches rather than overt 'teaching' that dominates the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let piety or moralizing spoil the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Lying Lover' (and adaptations) showed that 'earnestness in upholding truth and right did cause him to spoil the comedy' and that Steele 'had his play damned for its piety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep moral lessons from overwhelming plot, character, or comic effect; balance reforming or pious aims so they do not transform a comic work into mere morality-play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make theatrical writing bold enough for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The partners observed the play was 'like a picture in which the strokes were not strong enough to appear at a distance' — theatrical scenes must register before a popular assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stagework, use clear, bold strokes and emphatic characterization and action so distant or large audiences can perceive and respond; delicate literary subtleties may be lost in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subtlety to audience — delicate touches suit readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'touches being too delicate for every taste in a popular assembly' — many beauties 'escaped the audience' though they exist for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the level of subtlety depending on medium and audience: more delicate, refined humour may succeed in print or intimate settings but fail before a coarse or large public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations should suit contemporary morals and tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele altered Corneille's close 'in sharp accordance with that
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting older/foreign works, alter endings, tone or emphasis to accord with the sensibilities of a reforming or modern audience (e.g., changing romantic cross-marriage endings), but beware of changing form so much that the genre is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a natural and easy vein of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's play was praised as 'drawn after Molière's manner, and that an easy and natural vein of humour ran through the whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor humour that flows naturally from character and situation rather than forced similes, contrived repartees, or gratuitous witticisms intended solely to 'gain upon a false taste.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw characters from life without exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of a free-thinking exquisite is 'drawn from life without exaggeration, but with more than a touch of the bitter contempt Addison felt' — realistic portrayals are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid caricatured exaggeration when the goal is insight or satire; realistic, measured character-sketches preserve credibility and moral force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide actors with opportunities for meaningful action
rubrics_metrics.description: The work 'has given an opportunity in several of its parts for as just and good actions as ever I saw on the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes and roles that allow performers to enact moral intensity and varied character traits — meaningful actions and well-drawn moments enhance both acting and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance serious matters with diversion in periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Defoe: 'After our Serious Matters are over, we shall at the end of every Paper, Present you with a little Diversion...'; the periodical should mix instruction and amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essay-periodicals, follow sober or instructive content with lighter diversions to keep readers engaged while still addressing important topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure actions, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They do not design to expose Persons but things; and of them, none but such as more than ordinarily deserve it; they who would not be censurd by this Assembly, are desired to act with caution enough, not to fall under their Hands; for they resolve to treat Vice, and Villanous Actions, with the utmost Severity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target behavior and public acts rather than attacking individuals' private character; make moral critique impersonal and focused on public conduct to retain fairness and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment should include an element of severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele adapted a line in his Prologue: 'Pleasure must still have something that's severe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow some sternness, reproving element, or moral weight within pleasure or comedy so that entertainment also instructs or reforms rather than merely indulging taste.
